Key Takeaways

Tower Semiconductor fell 14% in the past week, mostly in a chip selloff after Intel's weak forecast that also hit Lumentum and Coherent.

Tower then posted record third-quarter revenue, up 33%, and guidance above estimates.

Tower targets a $1.1 billion annualized run rate from silicon photonics in the fourth quarter, 5x its 2025 revenue from it.

At 26x forward earnings, about its five-year average, the stock looks like a buy.

Tower Semiconductor (TSEM:NASDAQ) fell 14% in the past week. Most of the drop came in a chip selloff that started with a weak forecast from Intel (INTC:NASDAQ).

Intel did most of the damage

The worst day was Oct. 30, with no Tower news. The evening before, Intel forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $15.0-$16.0 billion, below expectations. Its CFO expects a PC slowdown through at least the first half of next year. Intel fell 35% over the week. Tower's fellow optical-chip stocks Lumentum (LITE:NASDAQ) and Coherent (COHR:NYSE) dropped 22% and 12%.

Intel's problem is PCs. Tower CEO Russell Ellwanger says Tower's growth comes from data-center infrastructure.

A record quarter didn't help

Before Monday's open, Tower reported third-quarter revenue of $526 million, up 33%. Tower guided fourth-quarter revenue to $600 million, ahead of the $579.7 million consensus.

"We are entering the strongest growth phase in our history," Ellwanger said in the release.

Analysts already expected Tower's normalized EPS to nearly triple from 2025 to 2027:

Tower Semiconductor (TSEM): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2029 (TIKR)

With guidance above consensus, I see no reason for analysts to cut.

TIKR tracks 9 analysts on Tower Semiconductor. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Tower Semiconductor, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Tower Semiconductor's Analyst Ratings

Silicon photonics is the whole story

Ellwanger targets a $1.1 billion annualized run rate from silicon photonics alone in the fourth quarter. Customers are also extending their contracts through 2029.

Lumentum and Coherent are seeing the same demand. On Oct. 26, StoneX initiated coverage of both at Buy, saying their laser capacity is sold out into 2029. So three AI optics suppliers are booked years ahead, and all three sold off with Intel anyway.

Tower's third-quarter capex of $191 million was slightly more than its $185 million of operating cash flow.

Is Tower a buy at half its June high?

At Monday's close, Tower traded at 26x forward earnings. That's right at its five-year average and far below the 84x it hit in June:

title: Did The Market Read Cerebras Stock Right?

Cerebras Systems (CBRS) stock fell 57.6% from August 4 to November 2, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 2.3%. Shares slid following the company's August 12 second-quarter report, and they dropped again in late September and early October as reports said Cerebras lost an OpenAI workload to Nvidia. The price appears to assume Cerebras's growth is less secure than it looked, so how much of that growth depends on OpenAI?

Much Of Cerebras's Backlog Comes From OpenAI

A large part of the business Cerebras has already signed depends on OpenAI. The company had $25.4 billion of contracted work still to deliver at June 30. On the August 12 call, management said none of it came from AWS or any other large cloud provider. September news reports said a significant amount of that backlog traces to a December agreement with OpenAI.

Management said on that same call that OpenAI will still be a meaningful portion of revenue in 2027, and that share will shrink over time as AWS and other customers grow.

The late-September news concerned the customer behind much of that backlog. News reports that week, including on October 2, said Cerebras lost a key workload for OpenAI's Ultrafast mode to Nvidia during the same week a lockup on early holders' shares expired. On October 5, OpenAI's chief executive called Cerebras a close partner, and the shares rose 11% in early trading. They still lost 42.1% between October 2 and November 2. Late in October, short seller Culper Research disclosed a position against Cerebras, and the shares fell 11.7% to a record low on November 2.

Cerebras Reported A Far Wider Loss In August

The losses have not narrowed yet. Cerebras reported revenue of $180 million for the quarter ended June 30, up from $103 million a year earlier but below the $193 million reported for the three months to March 31. The company's operating loss grew to $477 million from $15 million in the prior quarter, though management's own core operating loss was far smaller at $33.6 million. Gross margin fell to 14.2% from 44.6% three months earlier. News reports said the shares slumped more than 18% before trading opened on August 13 after the company missed key estimates.

On that core measure, revenue rose 103% to $209.9 million, but management expects weaker third-quarter margins. The company guided core operating margin to minus 25% to minus 23%, against minus 16% in the second quarter. For the full year, management raised its core revenue outlook to $880 million to $890 million. Management also called the third quarter the low point for core gross margin, with an improvement in the fourth as more of its own lower-cost systems come online.

We just published the list of the 10 Best and Cheap Stocks to Buy Heading into 2027 and Western Digital (NASDAQ:WDC) ranks 7th on this list.

Wall Street's AI trade took a hard hit on October 30. Reuters reported that a selloff in tech shares pushed MSCI's global index down 1.5%, after results from Intel and Amazon showed how much cash AI spending is burning. Intel fell 28.6%, and the Philadelphia semiconductor index lost more than 7%, its biggest one-day drop since late June. Alphabet's shares had already slid 12.6% a day earlier, after it reported that its AI spending pushed its cash flow negative.

The nervousness had been building. Reuters reported on October 15 that South Korea's KOSPI index, home to some of the world's largest chipmakers, fell roughly 8% in a single session. Saxo Bank chief investment strategist Charu Chanana said the Asian selloff looked less like a sudden deterioration in technology fundamentals and more like a repricing of the cost of capital.

READ ALSO 10 Best Robotics Stocks to Buy That Are More Than 30% On Sale

Rates are a large part of that story. Bloomberg reported on October 4 that benchmark 10-year Treasury yields sat near 5.3%, and Franklin Templeton Institute head market strategist Chris Galipeau said the conversation would change if they reached 6%. Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Robert Schiffman added that hyperscalers such as Meta, Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Oracle now have cash needs far beyond what they generate, which pushes them toward debt markets.

Western Digital made our list of the best and cheap stocks to buy for two reasons. First, its forward P/E is 9 and expected revenue growth rate for 2027 is nearly 47%. Second, it is one of the most popular stocks among hedge funds which is why WDC is one of the best cheap stocks to buy according to hedge funds.

Western Digital reported that fiscal first-quarter revenue rose 55% from a year earlier, above the range management had guided, and then pointed to something faster. It expects revenue growth of 66% to 72% in the current quarter, driven by cloud customers that now account for most of its sales and by steady demand for high-capacity drives.

Why Western Digital’s (WDC) Massive Quarter Is Only the Beginning

The profit side is improving even more quickly. Adjusted gross margin widened to 58.1%, because customers pay more per terabyte for denser drives and Western Digital is adding capacity by packing more data onto each drive instead of building more factories. Chief executive Irving Tan pointed to multi-year visibility from its largest customers. The company also expects to start volume shipments of its first heat-assisted recording drives in the first half of next year.

We just published the list of the 10 Best Tech Stocks for the Next 5 Years and Broadcom (AVGO) ranked 7th on this list.

Big Tech just had a week investors will remember. At its low on Friday, Alphabet had lost $477 billion in market value for the week, its worst week ever and the second-biggest weekly wipeout for any US-listed stock by Yahoo Finance's calculations, Yahoo Finance reported on October 30.

Most of the damage came Thursday, when the Google parent lost $475 billion in a single session after its third-quarter results. For October as a whole, Yahoo Finance calculated a loss of about $766 billion at Friday's low. That is the second-biggest monthly loss ever for a US-listed company, behind only SpaceX's roughly $822 billion drop in July.

5 Best "Moonshot" Tech Stocks to Buy According to Short Sellers

Photo by Arturo Añez on Unsplash

Heavy Losses Spread Beyond Alphabet

Alphabet wasn't alone. SpaceX, Intel and Nvidia each lost more than $100 billion in market value this week, according to Yahoo Finance. Intel fell as much as 30% on Friday after a weak outlook, its steepest drop in decades, and Amazon shed about $70 billion after reporting results Thursday. Software stocks took some of the sharpest hits in percentage terms, with ServiceNow and Fortinet down roughly 25% to 33%.

Nvidia was among the biggest losers. Our analysis of whether Nvidia can sustain its exceptional margins as it becomes more than a chipmaker looks at what keeps its profits so high.

UBS Argues Against Heading for the Exits

Not all the money left the market. Eli Lilly, Tesla and SK Hynix added about $370 billion in combined value over the same stretch, even as the Magnificent Seven stumbled, Yahoo Finance said.

UBS's chief investment office argued against retreating. Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, the bank's CIO Americas and global head of equities, wrote on Friday that further volatility does not make leaving markets an effective way to protect a portfolio from drawdowns. She said UBS still sees scope for equity gains overall and believes investors should focus on "building a resilient portfolio that includes exposure beyond tech."

The selloff also left Alphabet's price-to-earnings ratio at its lowest in more than a decade, Yahoo Finance noted. You might also be interested in reading our piece on why Alphabet's low P/E is misleading even as the AI opportunity looks real.

Broadcom supplies semiconductors and infrastructure software, and it has become a leading maker of the custom AI accelerators and networking chips that fill data centers. Investors like it because that AI business is growing faster each quarter.
